flagged.evidence: https://docs.docker.com/get-started/docker-overview/: "The Docker client and daemon can run on the same system, or you can connect a Docker client to a remote Docker daemon." But https://docs.docker.com/reference/cli/docker/: "If neither flag is set and no custom context exists, Docker uses default sockets: unix:///var/run/docker.sock on macOS/Linux".
flagged.problem: The statement "The docker CLI uses a local dockerd process when executing Docker commands" is true in the default setup, because the CLI connects to the local socket unless -H, DOCKER_HOST or a context says otherwise. The card is only false if you read in a "requires" or "always" that the wording does not contain, so an expert could defend True.
flagged.suggestedFix: Keep false and the factKey client-connects-remote-daemon. Statement: "The docker CLI must run on the same host as the Docker daemon it controls." Explanation: "The CLI can reach a remote daemon over SSH or TCP, selected with -H, DOCKER_HOST or a docker context. With none of these set, it uses the local daemon socket." Source: https://docs.docker.com/reference/cli/docker/

flagged.urlStatus: loads, official; the overview supports pull-then-create
flagged.evidence: https://docs.docker.com/reference/cli/docker/container/run/: docker run "runs a command in a new container, pulling the image if needed and starting the container"; --pull default "missing": "Pull the image if it was not found in the image cache, or use the cached image otherwise."
flagged.problem: This is a strawman. Nobody who has studied Docker thinks a container can start before its image is there, because a container is created from the image. The card teaches nothing. Its phrase "under the default pull policy" also hints at the real fact without testing it.
flagged.suggestedFix: Keep false. Statement: "By default, docker run pulls a newer image for a tag that already exists locally." Explanation: "The default --pull policy of docker run is missing: Docker pulls only when the image is absent locally and otherwise uses the cached copy. Use --pull always to check the registry first." Source: https://docs.docker.com/reference/cli/docker/container/run/ (this differs from sr6-12, which is about docker build --pull for base images).

flagged.evidence: https://docs.docker.com/get-started/docker-overview/: "A container is defined by its image as well as any configuration options you provide to it when you create or start it."
flagged.problem: "Two containers started from one image keep separate runtime settings" is vague: it does not say which settings, or separate from what. It is close to a truism, since each container is its own object. The explanation also does not explain the statement. Its idea that per-container config is independent of the image is already the fact behind sr2-03 (docker run -e leaves the image's ENV unchanged), so the card adds nothing.
flagged.suggestedFix: Replace with a true Engine architecture card. Statement: "Docker Engine relies on containerd to create, start and stop containers." Explanation: "dockerd hands the container lifecycle to containerd, which uses runc as its default runtime to start the container processes." Source: https://docs.docker.com/engine/daemon/alternative-runtimes/ ("Docker Engine uses containerd for managing the container lifecycle, which includes creating, starting, and stopping containers.")

sections.notes:
I checked all 12 r1 cards against their source pages, all of which loaded and are official. Quotes that settle the cards that pass:
- sr1-01 (false): "An image is a read-only template", plus the read-write filesystem as the container's final layer (overview).
- sr1-03 (false): "they all share the same kernel" and "A VM is an entire operating system with its own kernel" (what-is-a-container).
- sr1-04 (true): "Processes running within a container cannot see, and even less affect, processes running in another container, or in the host system" (/engine/security/).
- sr1-05 (true): "When you use these settings, Docker modifies the settings for the container's cgroup on the host machine" (resource_constraints).
- sr1-06 (false): "the client sends these commands to dockerd" (overview).
- sr1-07 (true): "communicate using a REST API, over UNIX sockets or a network interface" (overview).
- sr1-10 (false): "the Docker daemon and containers run in a lightweight Linux VM managed by Docker" (mac-permission-requirements).
- sr1-11 (true): "Docker Desktop includes the Docker daemon (dockerd), the Docker client (docker)..." (overview).
- sr1-12 (true): "It can be useful to commit a container's file changes or settings into a new image" (commit reference).

Minor points, not flagged:
1. sr1-04 (namespaces isolate) and sr1-05 (cgroups limit) are the two sides of the classic namespaces versus cgroups split. The SECTIONS line names both, so I kept both. sr1-05 is a fairly direct definition of cgroups, and its difficulty 3 is overrated: 2 would fit.
2. sr1-03 assumes the default runc runtime. An alternative runtime such as Kata gives a container its own kernel, but that is outside this deck's depth.
3. The overview page used for sr1-11 still lists Docker Content Trust among Docker Desktop's components. The card doesn't depend on it, but don't build any explanation from that list.
4. sr1-12 slightly hints at sr1-01, because commit is how container changes become an image. I judged them distinct facts.
5. After the suggested fixes, r1 still has 6 true and 6 false cards: the sr1-02 replacement stays true, and the sr1-08 and sr1-09 replacements stay false.

flagged.evidence: Run reference: --rm "Automatically remove the container and its associated anonymous volumes when it exits". Card sr8-04 (factKey anonymous-volume-rm-cleanup) says "`docker run --rm` removes an unshared anonymous volume when its container exits" and its explanation describes --rm cleanup at exit, so a player who has seen sr8-04 already knows sr2-02 is True. The flag name rm also makes the answer easy to guess.
flagged.problem: Rests on the same --rm cleanup-on-exit fact as sr8-04 and is close to a name giveaway. Section r2 has no card on restart policies other than on-failure, so the slot is better used for that.
flagged.suggestedFix: Replace with a TRUE card. Statement: "With --restart unless-stopped, a container you stopped manually stays stopped after the Docker daemon restarts." Explanation: "unless-stopped works like always, except that a stopped container (stopped manually or otherwise) is not restarted, even when the daemon restarts." URL: https://docs.docker.com/engine/containers/start-containers-automatically/ (quote: "Similar to always, except that when the container is stopped (manually or otherwise), it isn't restarted even after Docker daemon restarts.")

flagged.evidence: https://docs.docker.com/reference/cli/docker/container/run/: -e, --env and --env-file "set simple (non-array) environment variables in the container you're running, or overwrite variables defined in the Dockerfile". https://docs.docker.com/engine/containers/run/: "You can even override ... variables defined using a Dockerfile ENV instruction when building the image."
flagged.problem: Strawman. Nobody who has studied Docker thinks a runtime flag rewrites the stored image config. The misconception a learner could really hold is about precedence: does the image ENV beat -e?
flagged.suggestedFix: Replace with a FALSE card. Statement: "An image's ENV value takes precedence over a docker run -e value for the same variable." Explanation: "Values passed with -e or --env-file override variables the Dockerfile set with ENV, for that container only. The image itself stays unchanged." Keep the same URL (run reference).

flagged.evidence: Logs reference: "The docker logs --follow command will continue streaming the new output from the container's STDOUT and STDERR." https://docs.docker.com/engine/logging/: "By default, docker logs shows the command's STDOUT and STDERR." and "that application may send its output to log files instead of STDOUT and STDERR."
flagged.problem: Give-away. A player can read the answer from the flag name --follow, which works like tail -f. The real behaviour to test is that docker logs only shows stdout and stderr, so an app that writes only to files inside the container shows nothing.
flagged.suggestedFix: Replace with a TRUE card. Statement: "docker logs collects a container's STDOUT and STDERR, so an app that writes only to files inside the container shows nothing." Explanation: "By default docker logs shows the main command's STDOUT and STDERR. Servers that log to files must redirect them to those streams to appear there." URL: https://docs.docker.com/engine/logging/

sections.notes: All 12 r2 cards were checked against their source pages, and every page loaded and is official and current. Cards that pass: 01 (-d: 'starts the container without occupying your terminal window'); 04 (--entrypoint replaces the executable and 'clears out any default command set on the image'); 05 (create: 'creates a new container from the specified image, without starting it', initial status 'created'); 06 (stop: SIGTERM or STOPSIGNAL/--stop-signal, then SIGKILL after the timeout); 07 (on-failure: 'Restart the container if it exits due to an error, which manifests as a non-zero exit code'); 08 (rm --force: 'Force the removal of a running container (uses SIGKILL)'); 09 (exec 'runs a new command in a running container'); 11 (engine/containers/run: 126 'can't be invoked', 127 'can't be found'); 12 (resource_constraints: 'By default, a container has no resource constraints'). Minor observations, not flagged: card 01 is close to a giveaway (-d for detach) but the section explicitly lists it at easy level. The sr3-10 STOPSIGNAL card and sr2-06 test different facts. The suggested fixes keep the balance at 6 true and 6 false (02 true to true, 03 false to false, 10 true to true). The suggested 02 replacement should be checked against sr2-07 so the two restart-policy cards are not treated as one split. They are different policies and different triggers, so they are not mirrored.

flagged.evidence: The Here-Documents section of https://docs.docker.com/reference/dockerfile/ has its own example 'RUN <<FILE1 cat > file1 && <<FILE2 cat > file2 / I am / first / FILE1 ...'. Here a RUN heredoc's lines end up as files file1 and file2 in the built image. The page also says 'If the command only contains a here-document, its contents is evaluated with the default shell' and 'With COPY instructions, you can replace the source parameter with a here-doc indicator to write the contents of the here-document directly to a file.'
flagged.problem: The statement says a RUN heredoc stores its lines as a file and expects False. The official page shows a RUN heredoc whose lines are written to files in the image (cat > file1), so an expert could defend True. The answer depends on which command takes the heredoc, not on the heredoc itself.
flagged.suggestedFix: Keep the answer False and test the COPY side instead. Statement (82 chars): "`COPY <<EOF /app.sh` runs the heredoc lines in the default shell during the build." Explanation (156 chars): "A COPY heredoc writes the here-document content to the destination file, here /app.sh. A RUN heredoc with no command is the form the default shell executes." Same URL.

flagged.evidence: https://docs.docker.com/reference/dockerfile/ (LABEL): 'To view an image's labels, use the docker image inspect command.' The same section says: 'Labels included in base images (images in the FROM line) are inherited by your image. If a label already exists but with a different value, the most-recently-applied value overrides any previously-set value.'
flagged.problem: Anyone can guess the answer: an inspect command shows image metadata, and nobody who studied would answer False, so the card has no real misconception behind it. The card also leans on CLI output, which the depth rule calls trivia. LABEL has a more useful behaviour to test: inheritance from the base image.
flagged.suggestedFix: Keep the answer True. Statement (75 chars): "An image inherits the LABEL values set in the base image named in its FROM." Explanation (173 chars): "Labels in the base image carry over to the new image. A LABEL with the same key in your Dockerfile overrides the inherited value, since the most recently applied value wins." Same URL.

flagged.evidence: https://docs.docker.com/reference/dockerfile/ (WORKDIR): 'If a relative path is provided, it will be relative to the path of the previous WORKDIR instruction.' The same section says: 'If the WORKDIR doesn't exist, it will be created even if it's not used in any subsequent Dockerfile instruction.'
flagged.problem: The fact is correct, but the answer follows from what 'relative path' means: a relative path resolves from the current directory, which the previous WORKDIR set. This makes it close to a definition or truism card. The automatic creation of a missing WORKDIR teaches more, because learners often add RUN mkdir.
flagged.suggestedFix: Keep the answer True. Statement (70 chars): "WORKDIR creates the named directory when it is missing from the image." Explanation (139 chars): "If the WORKDIR path does not exist, the builder creates it, even when no later instruction uses it, so a separate RUN mkdir is unnecessary." Same URL.

sections.notes:
I checked all 12 r3 cards (sr3-01 to sr3-12, all in docker-fundamentals-b1.json) against https://docs.docker.com/reference/dockerfile/, which loads (HTTP 200) and is the current official page. I fetched it as raw text and read the passages myself. Pinned versions: BuildKit v0.33.1 and Dockerfile frontend 1.27.1 are the latest non-prerelease tags (GitHub API, 2026-09-30); 0.34.0-rc1 and 1.28.0-rc1 are prereleases. So 'BuildKit 0.33' in sr3-11 appliesTo is current.

Cards that pass, with the deciding quote:
- sr3-01: 'FROM instructions support variables that are declared by any ARG instructions that occur before the first FROM.'
- sr3-02: 'The RUN instruction will execute any commands to create a new layer on top of the current image.'
- sr3-03: 'Local tar archives are extracted by default' (ADD); for COPY, 'If the source is a file, the file and its metadata are copied to the destination.' The /build/building/best-practices/ ADD or COPY section states the COPY side more directly, if you want a stronger source.
- sr3-04: 'The shell form of ENTRYPOINT ignores any CMD or docker run command line arguments.' Technically Docker still appends CMD to the /bin/sh -c argv as positional parameters, but the docs call it 'ignores', so the card stands.
- sr3-05: 'Unlike ENV, an ARG variable is not embedded in the image and is not available in the final container.' This is a different fact from sr12-08 (ARG visible in docker history) and sr6-07 (ARG in the RUN environment).
- sr3-07: 'The EXPOSE instruction doesn't actually publish the port.'
- sr3-08: 'This can detect cases such as a web server stuck in an infinite loop and unable to handle new connections, even though the server process is still running.'
- sr3-10: 'It does not affect signals sent by keyboard shortcuts such as Ctrl+C, which sends SIGINT directly to the process regardless of the STOPSIGNAL setting.' This does not duplicate sr2-06.
- sr3-11: 'Use the syntax parser directive to declare the Dockerfile syntax version to use for the build. If unspecified, BuildKit uses a bundled version of the Dockerfile frontend.'

Balance: true statements average 70.0 characters and false 70.2. The section has 6 true and 6 false, and all three replacements keep the original answers, so the balance holds. No explanation is over 240 characters. sr3-01 and sr5-12 both deal with ARG scope but test different facts (global ARG in FROM versus automatic platform ARGs needing a declaration inside the stage). No other duplicates with other sections.

flagged.evidence: "When you invoke `docker build`, Buildx interprets the build options and sends a build request to the BuildKit backend." and "BuildKit resolves the build instructions and executes the build steps." (https://docs.docker.com/build/concepts/overview/). The card is correct, but sr4-02 (docker-build-wraps-buildx) tests the same docker build -> Buildx -> BuildKit chain, and sr4-02's explanation says word for word that "Buildx interprets the options and sends the build request to BuildKit". Anyone who learns sr4-02 already knows the answer to sr4-01.
flagged.problem: This card rests on the same client-to-backend fact as sr4-02, and sr4-02's explanation gives away its answer. It is also very easy: once you know Buildx is the client, the answer follows from the role names.
flagged.suggestedFix: Replace with a TRUE card on a separate fact from the same page. Statement: "BuildKit requests local context files from the client only when a build step needs them." Explanation: "The legacy builder always copied the whole local context up front. BuildKit asks Buildx for files, secrets and SSH sockets at the moment a step needs them." Source: https://docs.docker.com/build/concepts/overview/ ("BuildKit only requests the resources that the build needs when they're needed. The legacy builder, in comparison, always takes a copy of the local filesystem.")

flagged.evidence: "`docker-container`: creates a dedicated BuildKit container using Docker." (https://docs.docker.com/build/builders/drivers/). The fact is correct, but the driver's name already says it runs in a container.
flagged.problem: Name giveaway: a player who knows nothing about the subject answers True from the driver name "docker-container" alone. The card teaches nothing about how this driver behaves differently from the default.
flagged.suggestedFix: Replace with a TRUE card on behaviour, from the same page. Statement: "The docker-container driver keeps build results in its build cache until you pass --load or an output." Explanation: "Only the default docker driver loads images into the local image store automatically. Other drivers need --load, an --output option, or the default-load driver option." Source: https://docs.docker.com/build/builders/drivers/ ("With other drivers, the build result remains in the build cache if you don't specify an output."). This avoids the multi-platform question the prompt rules out.

sections.notes:
I checked all 12 r4 cards. I fetched every source page as raw markdown from docs.docker.com (build/concepts/overview, build/concepts/context, build/builders/drivers, engine/deprecated, build/checks); each returned 200 and is current official documentation. The section is balanced at 6 true and 6 false. True statements average 76.8 characters and false ones 81.3, a gap inside the 5-character limit. With both replacements the gap stays inside the limit (true about 85.2, gap about 3.9).

Cards that passed, with the sentence that settles each:
- sr4-02: overview page, "The docker build command is a wrapper around Buildx."
- sr4-03: context page, "the set of files that your build can access". An expert could point to --build-context, but a named context is itself a build context, so the false answer holds.
- sr4-04: "When you specify a remote Git repository, the repository and all submodules are included."
- sr4-05: "If you pass the URL to a remote tarball, the URL itself is sent to the builder ... The download operation will be performed on the host where the BuildKit daemon is running."
- sr4-06: "When you build without a filesystem context, Dockerfile instructions such as COPY can't refer to local files."
- sr4-07: "matching patterns ... are removed from the build context before it's sent to the builder."
- sr4-08: "A Dockerfile-specific ignore-file takes precedence over the .dockerignore file at the root of the build context if both exist."
- sr4-09: "In addition to the default build context ... you can also pass additional named contexts." I also checked the BuildKit dockerui source: the main context comes from the frontend input named "context", not from a --build-context, so the false answer holds.
- sr4-11: engine/deprecated, "Docker v23.0 now uses BuildKit by default to build Linux images". One edge case: if the Buildx component is missing (static CLI binaries), the CLI silently falls back to the legacy builder with a deprecation warning. That is not an ordinary install, so the false answer stands.
- sr4-12: build/checks, "Instead of executing the build steps, this command only runs the checks and reports any issues it finds." Volatility may_change is right because the feature is labelled Beta.

Minor points that did not need a flag:
- sr4-05: "before BuildKit starts" reads a little oddly, since BuildKit is already running. "Before the build starts" would be clearer.
- sr4-07: for Git contexts the builder has to apply .dockerignore after cloning, but the statement plainly means the local-directory case.
- sr4-04: the wording is close to the source sentence but is restructured, so not a near-copy.

No overlap with r1, r3, r5, r6 or r12: I searched every raw card for Buildx, BuildKit, driver and context terms.

flagged.evidence: Multi-platform page: "use the `--platform` flag to define the target platforms for the build output, such as `linux/amd64` and `linux/arm64`". Buildx reference (https://docs.docker.com/reference/cli/docker/buildx/build/): "When using docker-container driver with buildx, this flag can accept multiple values as an input separated by a comma. With multiple values the result will be built for all of the specified platforms and joined together into a single manifest list."
flagged.problem: This is a strawman. The statement lists two architectures and then says the build targets a single one, so nobody who has studied would answer True. The only official sentence about comma-separated values also ties them to the docker-container driver, which drifts toward the docker-driver multi-platform question the prompt forbids.
flagged.suggestedFix: Replace (answer false): "Without --platform, `docker buildx build` targets linux/amd64 even when the BuildKit daemon runs on arm64." Explanation: "The default target platform is the platform of the BuildKit daemon running the build, so an arm64 builder produces an arm64 image unless --platform says otherwise." Source: https://docs.docker.com/reference/cli/docker/buildx/build/ ("The default value is the platform of the BuildKit daemon where the build runs.")

flagged.evidence: "This installs the QEMU binaries and registers them with binfmt_misc, enabling QEMU to execute non-native file formats for emulation." and "Docker Desktop supports running and building multi-platform images under emulation by default. No configuration is necessary as the builder uses the QEMU that's bundled within the Docker Desktop VM."
flagged.problem: This is a definition card. Saying that QEMU emulation runs non-native binaries just restates what an emulator is, so the answer can be read from the word "emulation" and the card teaches nothing about Docker.
flagged.suggestedFix: Replace (answer true): "With Docker Desktop, building an arm64 image on an amd64 machine runs its RUN steps under QEMU emulation by default." Explanation: "Docker Desktop's builder uses the QEMU bundled in its VM, so foreign-architecture RUN steps execute under emulation, often far slower than native or cross-compiled builds." Keep the same URL.

flagged.evidence: "You can selectively copy artifacts from one stage to another, leaving behind everything you don't want in the final image." and "None of the build tools required to build the application are included in the resulting image."
flagged.problem: The answer is given away by `FROM scratch`. scratch is by definition an empty image, so anyone who knows the term rejects the statement. "automatically" also signals a false statement. The card does not test the real multi-stage misconception, which is what COPY --from brings along.
flagged.suggestedFix: Replace (answer false): "In a multi-stage build, the final image includes every layer of an earlier stage that it copies a file from." Explanation: "COPY --from adds only the copied files to the final stage as a new layer; the source stage's other layers, tools and caches stay behind." Keep the same URL.

flagged.evidence: "You can use the `COPY --from` instruction to copy from a separate image, either using the local image name, a tag available locally or on a Docker registry." Example on the page: "COPY --from=nginx:latest /etc/nginx/nginx.conf /nginx.conf"
flagged.problem: The statement copies the page's own example. The `:latest` tag marks the value as an image reference, which gives the answer away, so the card is close to a strawman. Its misconception field is also wrong: "COPY --from accepts sources declared as stages in the same Dockerfile" is a true fact, not a misconception.
flagged.suggestedFix: Replace (answer false): "`COPY --from=nginx:latest` needs nginx:latest pulled with docker pull before the build starts." Explanation: "When --from names an image rather than a stage, the builder resolves it itself, using a local tag or fetching it from the registry, just as FROM does." Misconception: "An external image used by COPY --from must be pulled manually first." Keep the same URL.

flagged.evidence: "By default, the stages aren't named, and you refer to them by their integer number, starting with 0 for the first FROM instruction. However, you can name your stages, by adding an AS <NAME> to the FROM instruction." The Dockerfile reference now documents only `COPY [--from=<image|stage|context>]`.
flagged.problem: The core fact (index 0 is the first FROM) is supported and correct. The clause "even when that stage has a name" is not stated on the cited page or in the Dockerfile reference, which describe indices only for unnamed stages. BuildKit does accept a numeric index for a named stage, but the whole card cannot be checked on an official page, and the explanation does not cover that clause.
flagged.suggestedFix: Replace (answer true): "`COPY --from=0` copies from the stage that the first FROM instruction in the Dockerfile starts." Explanation: "Unnamed stages are referenced by integer, starting at 0 for the first FROM; naming stages with AS keeps COPY --from working if stages are reordered." Keep the same URL.

sections.notes:
I checked all 12 r5 cards. All four cited pages load and are official docs.docker.com pages: multi-stage, multi-platform (dateModified 2026-04-16), the Dockerfile reference and the buildx build reference. The answers of all 12 are correct.

Passing cards and the source text that settles them:
- 01: "pick up where a previous stage left off by referring to it when using the FROM directive".
- 02: "The source path of COPY --from is always resolved from filesystem root of the image or stage that you specify."
- 05: --target stops at that stage.
- 06: "BuildKit only builds the stages that the target stage depends on" versus "The legacy Docker Engine builder processes all stages ... leading up to the selected --target".
- 08: "the registry returns the manifest list, and Docker automatically selects the correct variant based on the host's architecture".
- 11: "the FROM instruction is pinned to the native platform of the builder (using the --platform=$BUILDPLATFORM option)".
- 12: "These arguments are defined in the global scope so are not automatically available inside build stages or for your RUN commands. To expose one of these arguments inside the build stage redefine it without value."

Section balance is 6 true and 6 false. The suggested replacements keep each card's answer, so the balance holds.

Things that are not flags:
- Cards 11 and 12 both lean on platform ARG scope. Card 12 is also near r3-01 (a global ARG before FROM can be used in FROM), but neither card's answer gives away the other's, so I did not mark them as duplicates.
- The plan factKeys for 02 (copy-from-stage-name) and 12 (targetplatform-cross-compile) no longer describe what those cards test, which are path resolution and ARG redeclaration. The keys need relabeling, but this is not a content error.
- The appliesTo value "BuildKit 0.33" on 06, 09, 10, 11 and 12 should be checked against the Dockerfile frontend pinned in step 1.

flagged.evidence: https://docs.docker.com/get-started/docker-concepts/building-images/understanding-image-layers/ : "When you run a container from an image, a union filesystem is created where layers are stacked on top of each other, creating a new and unified view." The card's answer is correct, but it follows from the meaning of 'union filesystem' plus 'stacked layers' (definition card), and it is a near-paraphrase of that source sentence. The explanation only restates the statement. The section also has no card on the container's writable layer, which its scope names.
flagged.problem: This is a definition card and a near-copy of the source: a player can answer it from the term 'union filesystem' alone, and it teaches nothing about how the writable layer behaves.
flagged.suggestedFix: Replace (keeps answer TRUE): "With overlay2, a container's first write to a large image file copies the whole file into its writable layer." Explanation: "OverlayFS copies up at file level, so the first write to an image file copies the entire file into the container layer; later writes go to that copy." Source: https://docs.docker.com/engine/storage/drivers/overlayfs-driver/ ("all OverlayFS copy_up operations copy the entire file, even if the file is large and only a small part of it's being modified").

flagged.evidence: https://docs.docker.com/build/cache/optimize/ : "The cache mount is persisted across builds, so even if you end up rebuilding the layer, you only download new or changed packages." The answer is correct, but the statement says that a mount named 'type=cache' 'reuses package downloads', so a player can guess True from the word cache. It also ignores a caveat: reuse depends on the package manager keeping its downloads (for example the Debian image's docker-clean apt config).
flagged.problem: The answer can be read from the mount type's name. The fact itself is the obvious one.
flagged.suggestedFix: Replace (keeps answer TRUE): "By default, concurrent builds on one builder write to the same `RUN --mount=type=cache` directory at once." Explanation: "A cache mount's sharing option defaults to shared, so multiple writers use it concurrently; set sharing=locked to serialise them or private to give each its own mount." Source: https://docs.docker.com/reference/dockerfile/#run---mounttypecache ("sharing: One of shared, private, or locked. Defaults to shared. A shared cache mount can be used concurrently by multiple writers.").

flagged.evidence: https://docs.docker.com/build/cache/optimize/ : "--cache-from specifies remote caches for the build to use." The statement "--cache-from imports reusable cache data from an external location" restates the flag's name. Nobody who reads the flag would answer False, so it is a definition card with a name giveaway. The behaviour in --cache-from/--cache-to that is worth testing is the default export mode: https://docs.docker.com/build/cache/backends/ : "In min cache mode (the default), only layers that are exported into the resulting image are cached, while in max cache mode, all layers are cached, even those of intermediate steps."
flagged.problem: The answer can be read from the flag name. The card teaches no behaviour.
flagged.suggestedFix: Replace (keeps answer TRUE): "With its default mode, `--cache-to` exports cache only for layers that end up in the final image." Explanation: "The default mode=min caches only layers exported into the resulting image; mode=max also caches the layers of intermediate steps and stages, for more cache hits." Source: https://docs.docker.com/build/cache/backends/

flagged.evidence: https://docs.docker.com/build/cache/optimize/ : "When the instruction is done executing, the mounted files are not persisted in the final image, or in the build cache." The answer (False) is correct and supported. But 'can add ... after merely reading them' is a wording tell: 'merely' signals that the statement is false, and nobody who studied would think that reading a file copies it into the image (strawman). The trap 'a temporary build input ends up in the image' is also already used by sr3-12 (heredoc stored as a file) and sr12-10 (SSH key persisted from type=ssh), so this makes three false cards on one template, above the deck limit of two. sections.notes: I checked all 12 r11 cards: 6 true (01, 04, 05, 08, 10, 12) and 6 false (02, 03, 06, 07, 09, 11). All four suggested replacements keep the original answer, so the balance stays 6/6. I read every source as markdown from docs.docker.com (the .md variant of each page) and all of them loaded and are current. Cards that pass, with the sentence that settles each: 02 (\"Compose always uses the most recent schema to validate the Compose file, regardless of the `version` field\"); 03 (history page: \"Compose v5, released in 2025, is functionally identical to Compose v2\" and \"Compose v2 and v5 uses the Compose Specification\"); 05 (\"Compose creates a network named `<project-name>_default` and attaches all services to it\"); this card is easy but tests a real misconception, that services land on Docker's default bridge. 07 (\"On startup, Compose does not wait until a container is \\\"ready\\\", only until it's running\"); 08 (\"`restart: true` ensures that if `db` is updated or restarted due to an explicit Compose operation ... the `web` service is also restarted automatically\"); 09 (\"assigned ones only start/stop when their profile is active\"; the explanation correctly covers the exception for an explicitly targeted service); 11 (develop spec: rebuild \"recreates the service with the updated image\"; file-watch page: \"replaces the running service container\"); 12 (merge page: \"all paths in the files are relative to the base Compose file (the first Compose file specified with `-f`)\"). A minor caveat on 12: with --project-directory, relative paths resolve from that directory instead, but the doc states the rule as written, so it is not flagged. Context for the flags: the 06 replacement adds a second merging card, but it rests on a different fact from 12 (value concatenation versus path resolution). If sr11-10 is replaced as suggested, sr11-11 can stay as the only card about watch actions. The 04 replacement cites /compose/how-tos/project-name/, which the original card did not use.

flagged.evidence: run page: "Both flags support the value `ALL`, so to allow a container to use all capabilities except for `MKNOD`" one would use `--cap-add=ALL --cap-drop=MKNOD`. The fact is correct, but the answer is readable from the flag wording: dropping ALL removes the capabilities.
flagged.problem: Give-away. A player who knows nothing about Docker answers True from the words "drop ALL" and "removes". It does not test a behaviour a developer could get wrong.
flagged.suggestedFix: Replace (answer true): "By default, Docker starts a container's root user with a reduced set of Linux capabilities." Explanation: "Docker grants container root a restricted capability set, so it holds far less power than host root; --cap-add and --cap-drop adjust that set." Source https://docs.docker.com/engine/security/ ("By default, Docker starts containers with a restricted set of capabilities.")

flagged.evidence: run page: "The `--privileged` flag gives all capabilities to the container." and "Docker enables access to all devices on the host, and reconfigures AppArmor or SELinux to allow the container nearly all the same access to the host as processes running outside containers on the host." The answer is correct.
flagged.problem: Name give-away and near-strawman. A flag called "privileged" that "keeps the normal restrictions" reads as False to anyone. The real misconception, that privileged only means extra capabilities, goes untested.
flagged.suggestedFix: Replace (answer false): "On Linux, `--cap-add=ALL` gives a container the same host access as `--privileged`." Explanation: "`--privileged` grants all capabilities and also opens access to all host devices and relaxes AppArmor or SELinux confinement; `--cap-add=ALL` only adds capabilities." Same URL.

flagged.evidence: seccomp page: the default profile "disables around 44 system calls out of 300+" and is "an allowlist that denies access to system calls by default and then allows specific system calls." The answer is correct.
flagged.problem: Definition card. seccomp is by definition a system-call filter, so "a seccomp profile blocks selected system calls" follows from the term itself. The explanation only restates the statement.
flagged.suggestedFix: Replace (answer true): "Docker's default seccomp profile is an allowlist: system calls missing from it fail with an error." Explanation: "The default profile denies system calls by default and allows a listed set, so a syscall it does not name returns an error inside the container." Same URL.

flagged.evidence: Dockerfile reference: "The specified user is used for `RUN` instructions and at runtime runs the relevant `ENTRYPOINT` and `CMD` commands." The answer is correct.
flagged.problem: Give-away by wording. "USER app runs the process as app" restates the instruction's name, so a non-expert answers True without knowing anything.
flagged.suggestedFix: Replace (answer true): "`docker run --user 1000` overrides the user set by the image's USER instruction." Explanation: "USER sets the default user for the image, but the -u or --user option of docker run replaces it for that container." Source https://docs.docker.com/engine/containers/run/ ("you can override the `USER` instruction by passing the `-u` option").

flagged.evidence: Dockerfile reference: the SSH mount "allows the build container to access SSH keys via SSH agents, with support for passphrases"; target option: "SSH agent socket path. Defaults to /run/buildkit/ssh_agent.${N}". Build secrets page: "If the credential you want to use in your build is an SSH agent socket or key, you can use the SSH mount".
flagged.problem: Near-strawman: anyone who knows RUN mounts are temporary rejects "persists the key in the image". It also repeats card 09's "not placed in the final image" point. The wording "SSH agent key" is vague, and the reference never states the not-baked claim explicitly for ssh mounts.
flagged.suggestedFix: Replace (answer false): "`RUN --mount=type=ssh` copies the host's private key file into the build container." Explanation: "An SSH mount exposes an SSH agent socket to the RUN instruction; the private key stays in the agent on the client side." Same URL.

sections.notes:
All 12 r12 cards (in raw/docker-fundamentals-b3.json) were checked against their source pages. Every source URL loads, is official and current, and supports its card. No answer is wrong.

Quotes that confirm the cards that pass:
- 01: /engine/security/ says "Only trusted users should be allowed to control your Docker daemon" and gives the /host = / example.
- 02: /engine/security/rootless/ says "with userns-remap mode, the daemon itself is running with root privileges".
- 06: /engine/security/apparmor/ says "This profile is used on containers, not on the Docker daemon".
- 08: /reference/dockerfile/ says "Build arguments are visible in the docker history command and in max mode provenance attestations".
- 09: /build/building/secrets/ says the secret is "temporarily available inside the build container, for the duration of the build instruction".
- 11: /scout/explore/analysis/ says "When an image includes an SBOM attestation, Docker Scout uses it instead of generating one", and image analysis "extracts the Software Bill of Material".
- 12: /dhi/ lists, for Community too, "SLSA Build Level 3 provenance, signed SBOMs, VEX statements, and cryptographic signatures on every image".

The five flags are all weak_card (give-away, definition card or near-strawman). Each replacement keeps its card's answer, so the section stays at 6 true (01,03,05,07,09,12) and 6 false (02,04,06,08,10,11).

Duplicate check: sr3-05 (ARG does not persist in the image ENV) and sr6-08 (secret values stay out of the cache key) are separate facts from sr12-08 and sr12-09. Only r12 tests capabilities, seccomp, AppArmor and USER.

Minor point on 08: an ARG that no later RUN uses does not show up in docker history. The docs' plain statement "visible in docker history" still covers the card, so it is not flagged.

duplicates.why: Both test the same fact: containers on a shared network talk to each other on the CONTAINER_PORT, and publishing a host port plays no part. sr10-03 says peers need -p; sr11-06 says Compose peers use the published HOST_PORT. Each is false for the same reason, so knowing one answers the other. sr11-06 is the sharper Compose CONTAINER_PORT versus HOST_PORT card. sr10-03 is worded awkwardly ('need -p to connect over a container port').

These are the two sides of one distinction the prompt states as a single fact: the containerd image store is the default only on fresh Engine 29 installs, and upgraded daemons keep overlay2 until it is enabled. 'On fresh ... installs' in sr7-11 implies that upgrades behave differently, which answers sr7-12. sr7-12 tests the real misconception (an upgrade migrates automatically), so keep it.

Both rest on one fact: the host IP prefix of -p controls which host address the port binds to, and leaving it out means all addresses. sr10-06 is close to a truism (writing 127.0.0.1 binds to loopback), and its statement implies the default is not loopback, which gives away sr10-05. sr10-05 carries the misconception named in the prompt.

Both test that runtime configuration belongs to the container and not to the image. sr1-02 (two containers from one image keep separate runtime settings) is true and directly implies that sr2-03 (-e rewrites the image's stored ENV) is false. sr1-02 is also close to a truism.

conflictGroups.name: image-unchanged-by-runtime
conflictGroups.why: sr1-12 (docker commit is needed to turn container changes into a new image) and the sr1-01 explanation (the image stays read-only) together answer the false claims that container edits or -e mutate the image. sr1-02 answers sr2-03.

conflictGroups.name: client-daemon-remote
conflictGroups.why: The sr1-06 and sr1-08 explanations teach that the CLI only sends API requests to a daemon that can be remote. That hints at sr1-07 and sets up sr9-02, whose explanation in turn restates the remote-daemon model.

conflictGroups.name: linux-kernel-desktop-vm
conflictGroups.why: The sr1-03 explanation (Linux containers share the host's Linux kernel) implies sr1-10 is false. The sr1-10 explanation (Desktop runs its daemon inside a Linux VM) gives away sr1-11 (Desktop bundles dockerd).

conflictGroups.name: namespaces-cgroups
conflictGroups.why: These are the two sides of the namespaces (isolation) versus cgroups (limits) split. Seen together, each confirms the other by elimination.

conflictGroups.name: configured-resource-limits
conflictGroups.why: 'A configured CPU quota' (sr1-05) and 'a container's configured memory limit' (sr9-12) imply that limits exist only when set. That answers sr2-12 (Docker assigns a hard memory limit by default).

conflictGroups.name: run-rm-cleanup
conflictGroups.why: The sr8-04 statement 'docker run --rm removes an unshared anonymous volume when its container exits' assumes --rm removes the container, which is exactly what sr2-02 asks.

conflictGroups.name: volume-cleanup-scope
conflictGroups.why: The named versus anonymous cleanup rules overlap. The sr8-05 explanation (plain prune covers anonymous volumes and --all adds named ones) and the sr8-04 explanation (--rm cleans anonymous volumes) together point to named volumes surviving docker rm (sr8-03).

conflictGroups.name: stop-signal
conflictGroups.why: The sr3-10 explanation ('STOPSIGNAL configures Docker's stop signal') confirms the 'configured stop signal' in sr2-06. The sr2-06 explanation names SIGKILL as the forced kill, which sr2-08 tests for rm --force.

conflictGroups.name: arg-persistence
conflictGroups.why: These all ask where ARG values live. sr3-05 (ARG does not stay in the image env) can push a player towards believing sr12-08 (ARG secrets stay hidden from history). The sr6-07 explanation (ARG enters the RUN environment) and the sr3-01 global ARG card blur into each other.

conflictGroups.name: buildx-buildkit-roles
conflictGroups.why: The sr4-02 explanation ('Buildx interprets the options and sends the build request to BuildKit') is the sr4-01 statement almost word for word. sr4-01 and sr4-10 both describe BuildKit as the backend that runs builds.

conflictGroups.name: build-target-stages
conflictGroups.why: The sr5-06 explanation ('BuildKit builds the selected target and its dependencies') answers sr5-05 (--target makes that stage the build result).

conflictGroups.name: build-mount-not-in-image
conflictGroups.why: All three use the same idea, that RUN --mount content is temporary and stays out of the image. The sr12-09 explanation ('rather than placing it in the final image') answers sr12-10 (SSH key persisted) and sr6-10 (bind inputs added).

conflictGroups.name: build-secret-handling
conflictGroups.why: Both are about RUN --mount=type=secret. Seeing secrets described as one-instruction temporary mounts nudges a player towards concluding that secret values are outside the cache key.

conflictGroups.name: image-reference-parsing
conflictGroups.why: The sr7-01 explanation says 'team is the namespace' and the registry is the dotted host, which answers sr7-02 (myteam is not the registry host). sr7-02 and sr7-03 both explain the docker.io and library defaults.

conflictGroups.name: digest-pinning
conflictGroups.why: sr7-06 teaches that a digest pins an immutable image version. That makes sr7-09 (docker pull accepts name@sha256:...) a giveaway.

conflictGroups.name: containerd-store-engine29
conflictGroups.why: This is a mirrored true and false pair covering fresh installs versus upgrades. Each answers the other.

conflictGroups.name: same-path-shared-mounts
conflictGroups.why: sr8-02 and sr9-11 share one false template (two containers share an anonymous volume or tmpfs because they use the same path), so one answers the other. sr8-11 (two containers mount one volume) sits right next to them and confuses the line between them.

conflictGroups.name: auto-create-missing-mount-source
conflictGroups.why: sr9-01 (-v creates a missing host directory) strongly hints that -v also creates a missing named volume (sr8-01, false 'fails').

conflictGroups.name: read-only-mounts
conflictGroups.why: The sr9-05 explanation ('ro makes the bind mount read-only inside the container') answers sr8-08. sr9-04 (writable by default) and sr9-05 are the default and the ro option of the same mount.

conflictGroups.name: volume-populate-vs-bind-obscure
conflictGroups.why: These are the two sides of one volume versus bind distinction: an empty volume is pre-populated, while a bind mount obscures the content. Shown together, they contrast and give each other away.

conflictGroups.name: bind-propagation
conflictGroups.why: Both statements hinge on rshared bind propagation. The sr9-07 explanation (the default is rprivate) and the sr9-08 explanation (propagation does not work with Desktop) overlap.

conflictGroups.name: peer-traffic-and-publishing
conflictGroups.why: The sr10-03 and sr11-06 explanations both say that -p or HOST_PORT is only for outside access, which also confirms sr10-04's mapping. The sr3-07 explanation (publishing needs a runtime port mapping) overlaps.

conflictGroups.name: publish-host-address
conflictGroups.why: sr10-06 (giving 127.0.0.1 binds loopback) implies the default is not loopback, which answers sr10-05.

conflictGroups.name: compose-version-confusion
conflictGroups.why: The sr11-02 explanation (Compose validates against the latest schema whatever the version says) and sr11-01 (v5 reads compose.yaml per the Compose Specification) together imply that v5 uses no new file format (sr11-03).

conflictGroups.name: compose-watch-actions
conflictGroups.why: This is close to a mirrored pair. The sr11-10 explanation stresses that sync works 'while the service container keeps running', and sr11-11 falsely gives rebuild that same keep-running behaviour.

conflictGroups.name: sbom-products
conflictGroups.why: This is a weak hint. 'DHI ship signed SBOMs' sits next to 'Scout skips images lacking an SBOM attestation' and suggests attached SBOMs are a precondition.

4. Recurring false templates:
(a) 'Two containers ... share the same X [because of the same path or network]' is false 3 times (sr8-02, sr9-11, sr10-03) against 2 true 'Two containers' cards (sr1-02, sr8-11). This exceeds the prompt's two-per-template cap if sr10-03 counts.
(b) 'A runtime action modifies the image' is false twice (sr1-01, sr2-03), which is at the cap.
(c) 'Build-time input ends up persisted in the image' is false 3 times (sr3-05 ARG in env, sr6-10 bind input added, sr12-10 SSH key persisted), and sr12-08 is its inverse. That is over the cap.
(d) 'Feature A is given sibling B's job' (the explanation names the sibling) is false in sr3-03 (COPY given ADD's job), sr10-10 (ipvlan given macvlan's), sr11-11 (rebuild given sync's), sr12-02 (userns-remap given rootless), sr6-12 (--no-cache given --pull's) and sr4-02 (docker build vs Buildx). A player who sees two near-synonymous features named can guess false.
(e) 'With default X, Docker does the restrictive or safe thing' is false in sr2-12 (memory limit), sr10-05 (localhost), sr12-04 (privileged keeps restrictions) and sr12-06 (AppArmor protects dockerd).

5. Length: statement averages are within 5 characters in every section, but false runs longer in r1 (+4.7), r4 (+4.5), r10 (+4.5) and r6 (+4.3), right at the limit. Explanations for false cards are much longer in r7 (+25.6), r5 (+16), r6 (+13) and r11 (+11). This matters only if explanations are previewed.

6. Strawmen and truisms that are answerable without knowledge:
- sr8-08 ('read-only mount can still update files')
- sr5-07 ('scratch automatically includes earlier tools')
- sr5-09 ('a two-platform list targets a single architecture')
- sr10-04 ('-p 8080:80 maps 8080 to 80')
- sr2-01 (-d detaches)
- sr1-02 (separate runtime settings)
